prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat bands

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged in substance: a single-part prize for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The reason is the one that matters most to me as a theorist of electronic structure. A parameter-free continuum model (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011) said that one geometric knob, the twist angle, would quench the kinetic energy of the bands, and seven years later correlated insulators and superconductivity appeared at that angle in a carbon-only system (Jarillo-Herrero and collaborators, 2018). Many independent groups have since reproduced the phases and extended the idea to twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides and to fractional Chern states. The existence and tunability of the flat-band platform is secure, and that is the discovery. The pairing mechanism is a question about what happens on top of the platform, in the same way that the mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity was open when cuprates were recognised. I have changed one thing: in round 1 I called a two-name MacDonald plus Jarillo-Herrero version defensible, and after reading Mehlig and Olsson I now withdraw that. The 2011 prediction is a joint paper with Bistritzer as first author, and I see no principled rule that removes him while keeping the other two. My final position is the three listed names, with a citation that names the prediction and the observed phases and does not claim to honour everyone who worked on the experiments.
statement.case_against: The credit set is imperfect and I do not think a citation can repair it. Yuan Cao and Valla Fatemi, the first authors of the 2018 experiments, Dean, Young, Ashoori and others on moire platforms, and the earlier twisted-bilayer band-structure work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto all fall outside a three-name cap. The unresolved nature of the superconducting pairing and of several correlated states makes this the least settled of the leading candidates, and a reasonable member could conclude that the optical lattice clock (B061), with its decades of confirmation and two-name credit, is the more finished achievement. I weigh the clock case as strong and I would not regard it as a poor outcome. I remain with B013 because I weight a new regime of matter anticipated by calculation and delivered by experiment above cleanliness of attribution, and I do not think the credit gaps are larger than those the clock case carries (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, PTB, NIST and SYRTE).

responses.point: Mehlig argues that dropping Bistritzer would credit the continuum model to MacDonald alone although the 2011 paper is joint with Bistritzer as first author, and that there is no principled reason to remove him while keeping the other two. He also says he now weighs the timing concern less.
responses.response: I accept this and change my own round-1 position. A two-name version would leave a prediction without its first author, and the rule I would otherwise use, crediting the decisive prediction and the decisive experimental programme, gives exactly the three listed names. I also agree with his reading of maturity: what is rewarded is the prediction and the observed phases, which have been reproduced widely, not an explanation of pairing. Where I still differ is on his remark that earlier work by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is only history. It showed that twisted bilayers have reconstructed bands, but it did not identify the magic-angle flat-band condition or predict strong correlation, so the omission is defensible, but I would still want the citation worded around the magic-angle prediction so that it does not claim to settle priority.

responses.point: Pearce finds the prediction-then-observation structure persuasive and accepts a two-name configuration, but says B013 is less ready than clocks because the interpretation of the correlated and superconducting states is still moving, whereas the lattice-clock claim is settled by repeated measurement. He says he would go to B013 if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize.
responses.response: I agree that the clock claim is more settled, and this is the strongest argument for B061. I do not think it is a maturity argument against B013, though. What has to be settled is the discovery, and flat bands, correlated insulators and superconducting domes in twisted bilayers have been measured by transport, tunnelling and compressibility experiments in many laboratories. The part still moving is the interpretation. Prizes in this field have been given before the mechanism was understood. I also note that you moved to B061 by reading the support count, and I would ask that the final vote rest on the scientific criterion instead. For a criterion the chair asked us to state: I weight the novelty of the regime opened first, and the completeness of the confirmation second.

responses.point: Lindroth rests the case for B061 on atomic-structure physics she can judge directly (magic wavelength, blackbody shift), argues that the two-name credit is clean and that the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover the neutral-atom lattice clock, and says that if the committee prefers a new field to a new level of measurement, B013 is stronger.
responses.response: I take the atomic-physics argument seriously. As someone who works with first-principles polarisabilities, I find it persuasive that the magic wavelength and the blackbody correction are calculable and checked against experiment, and that makes the 10^-18 claim credible. I also accept that the 2005 comb prize enabled but did not recognise the lattice clock. Your own criterion, a prize for a new field of physics, is the one on which I place B013 first. I do not think attribution cleanliness should decide the ranking by itself, and I note that the clock credit also leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, so the difference in cleanliness is smaller than the two-name count suggests. If the committee settles on the clock I would support it, and I have kept B061 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Kroll presents the clock as a distinct, mature successor to the 2005 and 2012 prizes, with concrete consequences (redshift tests, varying constants, relativistic geodesy) and compact attribution, and says it is a convergent choice since colleagues who rank other candidates first still place it in their top three.
responses.response: I agree that the clock is a convergent choice and that the consequences are real. The disagreement is on the criterion and not on facts, so I would not call it a bias. Convergence across members is a signal, but support counts should not stand in for the scientific comparison, and B013 has the same breadth of opening support. I would ask whether the redefinition of the second is a reason to wait, since a prize now recognises a capability and a decision that the metrology community has not yet taken. I do not think it is a reason against, but it is why I read the clock as a prize for refinement of a known measurement and the moire case as a prize for something nobody could previously measure.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B061 after the opening ballots, and in round 1 said that dropping Bistritzer from a theory-experiment pair would sever the prediction she values and that keeping all three leaves the first author of the experiments out while a group leader is credited.
responses.response: This is the tension I accepted in round 1, and it is real: Cao is the first author of the experimental papers and the three-name cap excludes him. I now think the principled answer is to credit the leader of the experimental programme and the authors of the prediction, as the committee has done in other discovery prizes, and to say plainly in the citation which contributions are honoured, so that nobody reads the list as a verdict on who did the bench work. The alternative would be to honour two theorists and no experimentalist, which would turn a discovery that nature delivered into a prize for a model alone. Your preference for the clock is a fair reading of the same facts, and I would welcome your view on whether the wording above answers the fairness concern.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B013 first and says the open pairing mechanism concerns follow-on physics and that the omissions cannot be repaired within a three-name cap, so the citation should name the prediction and the observed phases.
responses.response: I agree and we are aligned on wording. I would add one point to your caution about maturity: the existence of the platform has been established by independent experiments, so what is still unsettled is which theory explains the superconducting state. I would keep the citation to the magic-angle flat bands and the observed correlated and superconducting states, and not use phrases that claim an explanation of pairing or founding a field, because the second is a judgement for later.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts a three-name credit that leaves out Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and others, or prefers the cleaner two-name B061 allocation.
Whether the unresolved mechanism of the superconductivity is only a matter of citation wording, as I judge, or a reason to defer recognition one more year.
Whether the redefinition of the second, once it happens, changes the relative standing of B061, which would change my first alternative.
I rely on my own recollection of the chronology and have not verified it independently.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie with any credited name on B013, B061 or B019. My own research in electronic structure and magnetism is adjacent to moire flat-band physics, and I disclose that proximity. The chair's summary records it and no recusal is proposed.
